title: Field investigation associates norovirus GII outbreak at Chinese university with canteen dining
excerpt: A field investigation of 215 gastroenteritis cases at a Chinese university associated the outbreak with dining at one canteen and found norovirus GII in 16 of 66 tested samples.

content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, October 20, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Field investigation associates norovirus GII outbreak at Chinese university with canteen dining by October 20, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 Infected Canteen Workers Traced as Source of Norovirus GII.17 Outbreak at Chinese University Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A field investigation of an acute gastroenteritis outbreak at a university in Jinhua, China, identified 215 cases from December 14 to 24, 2024, with an overall attack rate of 0.48%. Most affected people experienced diarrhea and vomiting. The study authors reported that the epidemic curve was consistent with continuous exposure to a common source followed by secondary transmission, while laboratory testing found norovirus GII in 16 of 66 clinical, environmental and food-handler samples. Four positive samples were sequenced and identified as GII.17; genotypes for the other positive samples, including the sample described as the index case, were not available. The investigation combined a descriptive description of cases by time, symptoms and location with case–control and retrospective cohort studies examining dining exposures, hygiene behaviors and illness risk. The first-floor canteen in Zone A had the highest reported attack rate, at 1.14%, compared with 0.56% in Zone B and 0.42% in Zone C. The relative risk for Zone A versus Zone C was 2.71 (95% confidence interval, 1.89–3.89). Dining at the Zone A first-floor canteen was the primary food-related risk factor identified in the analysis, with an odds ratio of 18.85 (95% CI, 2.44–145.39). The reported association increased with the number of meals consumed: relative risks were 1.82 for two or three meals and 3.45 for more than three meals. Poor hand hygiene was also associated with illness, with an odds ratio of 14.60. Of the 66 tested samples, six positive samples came from canteen workers, including two from people without symptoms. Six infected workers continued working through December 20, and four were cashiers who handled takeaway packaging. Investigators also observed improper glove use and inadequate tableware disinfection in the canteen environment. The authors stated that the epidemiological pattern, together with the laboratory and environmental findings, strongly implicated foodborne transmission involving infected canteen staff, followed by person-to-person spread. The investigation did not establish a complete transmission chain, and the positive samples that were not sequenced could not be assigned a genotype. The study’s findings were based on the supplied published abstract and were reported in BMC Infectious Diseases as accepted research subject to further editing. Its scope was limited to one university outbreak and the available laboratory sequencing results. The investigators proposed staff health monitoring, standardized work practices, hand-hygiene promotion and prompt disinfection as components of outbreak control, but the abstract did not report a controlled evaluation of those measures or their effectiveness. (2026). An outbreak of Norovirus GII gastroenteritis in a Chinese university: investigating transmission patterns and implications for public health interventions.
